items.title: G14: unchecked wrap-around versus checked overflow
items.body:
C# integer arithmetic is **unchecked by default**. `int.MaxValue + 1` does not fit in 32 bits, so it silently wraps around to the smallest int, -2147483648. No error, no warning. Wrapping the expression in `checked(...)` turns on overflow checking for it, and the same addition throws `OverflowException`. You can also turn checking on for a whole project with the CheckForOverflowUnderflow build setting.

Why the others are wrong:
- `checked` applies to integer arithmetic. The guide's point about `decimal` is the reverse: decimal always throws on overflow, checked or not.
- Without `checked`, the plain addition does not throw; it wraps.
- `int + int` stays `int`; C# does not promote it to `long`, and `checked` does change behaviour.

excerpts.quote: int x = int.MaxValue; Console.WriteLine(x + 1); Console.WriteLine(checked(x + 1)); ``` **Answer:** `-2147483648`, then an `OverflowException`.
**Why:** C# is **unchecked by default** — it silently wraps. `checked` (or the project-wide `<CheckForOverflowUnderflow>`) throws. `decimal` always throws on overflow regardless.

items.title: G21: why await on WhenAll shows only the first exception
items.body:
Both tasks throw. The task returned by `Task.WhenAll` does collect both failures in an `AggregateException`. But `await` does not throw that wrapper: it unwraps it and rethrows only the **first** inner exception. So the catch prints `A`, and B is silently lost to this catch. To see every failure you keep a reference to the WhenAll task and read `Task.Exception.InnerExceptions` on it.

Why the others are wrong:
- WhenAll does not swallow anything; the await throws.
- Only one exception reaches the catch; await does not throw the AggregateException listing both.
- "One or more errors occurred" would be the AggregateException's own message, but `await` does not throw the wrapper; it throws the first inner exception, whose message is A.

excerpts.quote: var t1 = Task.Run(() => throw new Exception("A")); var t2 = Task.Run(() => throw new Exception("B")); try { await Task.WhenAll(t1, t2); } catch (Exception ex) { Console.WriteLine(ex.Message); }

**Why:** `WhenAll`'s task holds an `AggregateException` with both, but `await` unwraps and rethrows only the **first**. Exception B is silently lost. To see them all: catch, then read `Task.Exception.InnerExceptions` on the WhenAll task.

items.title: Concept: the four ideas behind most C# output gotchas
items.body:
The file's closing section says most of its snippets come from four ideas. Learn the ideas, and the individual snippets become easier to reason about:

- **Value vs reference**: when does assigning, passing or reading something give you a copy, and when a second name for the same object?
- **Deferred execution**: when does a LINQ query's code actually run, and what values does it see then?
- **Compile-time vs runtime dispatch**: which choices (operators, overloads, virtual methods) are fixed when the code compiles, and which depend on the real object at runtime?
- **Three-valued logic**: what can a comparison mean when one side is null?

When you read a snippet, first name which of these ideas it tests, and write the question above for that idea next to it. Then predict, and only then read the Answer and the Why.

excerpts.quote: you get there by understanding value vs reference, deferred execution, compile-time vs runtime dispatch, and three-valued logic.

readMore.why: The Value vs reference section shows the copy rule in several shapes.
The LINQ section, for deferred execution.

items.title: G4: array element versus List indexer for a struct
items.body:
An array indexer `arr[0]` gives you the element itself (a reference to its storage). So `arr[0].X = 5;` changes the struct stored in the array, and printing it gives 5.

A List indexer `list[0]` is a property: a method that **returns a copy** of the struct. Setting `.X` on that copy would change a temporary and do nothing useful. The compiler knows this and refuses: "Cannot modify the return value ... because it is not a variable." It is a compile error, not a runtime one.

Why the others are wrong:
- The array line does change the stored element; and the List line does not compile at all.
- Structs in a List or an array are stored as values, not boxed.
- The compiler catches it, so nothing happens at runtime.

excerpts.quote:
struct P { public int X; } var arr = new P[] { new P { X = 1 } }; arr[0].X = 5; Console.WriteLine(arr[0].X); var list = new List

{ new P { X = 1 } }; // list[0].X = 5; ← what happens here?

**Answer:** `5` for the array. The `List` line is a **compile error**: "Cannot modify the return value of `List

.this[int]` because it is not a variable."

items.title: G1: why every lambda in the for loop prints 3
items.body:
A `for` loop has **one** variable `i`, shared by all iterations. Each lambda captures that variable itself, not a copy of its current value. The lambdas run only later, in the `foreach`, after the loop has finished. When the loop ends, `i` is 3 (that is what stopped the loop). All three lambdas read the same `i`, so the output is 333.

The fix is to copy into a local inside the loop (`int copy = i;`), or to use `foreach`, which since C# 5 gets a fresh variable each iteration and would print 012.

Why the others are wrong:
- `i` is not 0 when the lambdas run; it has been incremented to 3.
- 012 is the `foreach` (or local copy) behaviour, not this `for` loop.
- Capturing a loop variable is legal; the closure keeps it alive.

excerpts.quote: var actions = new List<Action>(); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) actions.Add(() => Console.Write(i)); foreach (var a in actions) a();

**Why:** the `for` loop has **one** variable `i`; all three lambdas capture the same variable, and by the time they run it's 3. Change `for` to `foreach (var i in Enumerable.Range(0,3))` and it prints `012` — since C# 5, `foreach` declares a *fresh* variable per iteration. Fix for `for`: copy into a local (`int copy = i;`) inside the loop.

items.title: G5: why Inc() on an unboxed struct changes nothing
items.body:
`object boxed = new Counter();` puts a copy of the struct in a box on the heap. `(Counter)boxed` **unboxes**, and unboxing makes another copy: a temporary value outside the box. `.Inc()` increments that temporary, which is then thrown away. The box still holds `Value = 0`. The last line unboxes a fresh copy and prints 0. No error tells you the change was lost, which is why mutable structs and boxing are a dangerous mix.

Why the others are wrong:
- The box really holds a Counter, so the cast succeeds; there is no InvalidCastException.
- 1 would need the increment to reach the boxed value; it only reached a copy.
- Calling a method on the unboxed temporary is allowed; it compiles.

excerpts.quote: struct Counter { public int Value; public void Inc() => Value++; } object boxed = new Counter(); ((Counter)boxed).Inc(); Console.WriteLine(((Counter)boxed).Value);
**Why:** unboxing **copies** the struct out of the box. You incremented a temporary that was thrown away. Mutable structs + boxing = changes that vanish with no error.

items.title: G17: what a virtual call in a base constructor sees
items.body:
`new Derived()` runs in this order in C#:

1. Derived's **field initializers**: `_fromInitializer = "init"`.
2. Base's constructor, which calls the virtual `Print()`.
3. Derived's constructor body: `_fromCtor = "ctor"`.

The virtual call in step 2 goes to `Derived.Print`, because the object really is a Derived. At that moment step 1 is done but step 3 is not. So it prints `init / null`. The guide's lesson: never call a virtual method from a constructor, because the object is not finished yet.

Why the others are wrong:
- "null / null" is what Java would print, where the superclass constructor runs before field initializers. C# runs initializers first.
- "init / ctor" would need the derived constructor body to have run already; it has not.
- "Base" would mean no virtual dispatch, but `Print` is overridden and the call dispatches to Derived.

excerpts.quote: class Base { public Base() { Print(); } protected virtual void Print() => Console.WriteLine("Base"); } class Derived : Base { private string _fromInitializer = "init"; private string _fromCtor; public Derived() { _fromCtor = "ctor"; } protected override void Print() => Console.WriteLine($"{_fromInitializer ?? "null"} / {_fromCtor ?? "null"}");
the derived class's *field initializers* run **before** the base constructor

items.title: G16: return values, references and finally
items.body:
When `return x;` runs, the value to return is worked out and stored *first*. Then `finally` runs. In F, `finally` sets the local `x = 2`, but the stored return value is already 1, so F() returns 1.

G is different because it returns a **reference** to a list. The stored return value is that reference. `finally` then calls `l.Add(1)` on the same list object. The caller gets the reference and sees the list as it is now, with one element. So G().Count is 1. Same rule, different result, because of value versus reference.

Why the others are wrong:
- Reassigning `x` in finally is too late; the int has already been copied out.
- This is legal C#; nothing throws.
- The list is not empty: finally ran before the caller looked at it, and it changed the shared object.

excerpts.quote: static int F() { int x = 1; try { return x; } finally { x = 2; } } static List<int> G() { var l = new List<int>(); try { return l; } finally { l.Add(1); } }

**Why:** the return **value** is evaluated and stashed before `finally` runs, so reassigning the local `x` is too late. But `G` returns a *reference* — the object it points to is mutated in `finally`, and the caller sees it. Value vs reference, one more time.

items.title: Start here: the C# interview plan and its gotcha snippets
items.body:
This repo is a study plan for moving from junior to mid-level .NET developer. Every quiz in this pack comes from one file: **04-question-vault/12-code-output-gotchas.md**, a set of short "what does this print?" C# snippets, each with an Answer and a Why.

Read in this order:

- **UPSKILL-PLAN.md**, the TL;DR: what the plan is and why it insists you attempt things yourself first.
- **04-question-vault/00-overview.md**: the file list, "The answer shape" and the "Three drill modes". It tells you when the depth files are worth your time.
- **12-code-output-gotchas.md**, one section at a time: Closures & capture, Value vs reference, Equality & strings, Numbers, Control flow, Async, LINQ. Cover the Answer line, commit to a prediction, then read the Why.
4. Later, **04-efcore.md** and **13-spot-the-bug.md** for depth.

Each quiz starts with "Goal:", the skill the snippet trains. The best way to learn these is the file's own advice: when you get one wrong, paste the snippet into a small console app and run it.

excerpts.quote: **Answers are inline — cover them.**
**The real drill:** for every one you miss, *run it*. Watching it print the wrong thing on your own machine is what makes it stick.

readMore.why: The full ten-week plan this vault belongs to.
How the question vault is organised and drilled.

items.title: G25: Sum, FirstOrDefault and Average on an empty list
items.body:
Each method answers "what is the result for no items?" differently:

- `Sum()` of nothing is 0, a sensible empty total.
- `FirstOrDefault()` returns the *default* of the element type. For `int` that is 0, not null; an `int` cannot be null.
- `Average()` of nothing has no meaningful value, so it throws `InvalidOperationException: Sequence contains no elements` (so do `Max`, `Min` and `First`).

The trap the guide points out: with `int`, `FirstOrDefault` cannot tell "empty" from "found a 0". Use `int?` or `Any()` first.

Why the others are wrong:
- Sum and FirstOrDefault do not throw on empty input.
- Sum does not throw, and Average throws rather than returning NaN.
- FirstOrDefault on `int` is 0, not null, and Average does not return 0.

excerpts.quote: var empty = new List<int>(); Console.WriteLine(empty.Sum()); Console.WriteLine(empty.FirstOrDefault()); Console.WriteLine(empty.Average()); ``` **Answer:** `0`, `0`, then `InvalidOperationException: Sequence contains no elements`.
`Sum` of nothing is defensibly 0; `Average` of nothing is genuinely undefined so it throws

items.title: G15: comparing a null int? with a number
items.body:
`int?` operators are "lifted": they work on nullable values, with a rule for null. For comparisons, if either side is null the answer is `false`, because the result is *unknown*. So `a > 5` is false and `a <= 5` is also false, even though for real numbers one of them must be true. That is three-valued logic, the same as SQL's NULL. The practical trap: `if (a > 5) ... else ...` sends null into the else branch, which the author may not have meant.

Why the others are wrong:
- `a <= 5` is not true; every ordering comparison with null is false.
- Comparisons return `bool`, not null. (Arithmetic such as `a + 1` is the one that gives null and prints an empty line.)
- Comparing does not read `.Value`, so nothing throws.

excerpts.quote: int? a = null; Console.WriteLine(a + 1); Console.WriteLine(a > 5); Console.WriteLine(a <= 5); Console.WriteLine(!(a > 5)); ``` **Answer:** *(empty line)*, `False`, `False`, `True`
**both** `>` and `<=` are false because the comparison is *unknown*

items.title: Concept: how to drill gotchas so they stick
items.body:
Reading answers top to bottom feels like progress but teaches little. The overview's third mode, **"Gotcha gauntlet"**, is the drill for this file: someone (or an AI quizzer) gives you one snippet, you say what it prints and why, and only then do you see the answer. If you were wrong, you must explain the real mechanism before moving on.

The overview also gives an **answer shape** for interviews: claim, why, tradeoff, and an example from your own project. For a gotcha, the claim is the output, the why is the mechanism, and the tradeoff is how to avoid the trap in real code (for example "materialize once" or "use a fresh local").

The file's last table gives a rough reading of your score out of 32. Treat it as a guide to what to drill next, not as a grade. Log each miss by its number (such as G12) so you can come back to exactly that snippet.

excerpts.quote: > Give me one snippet at a time from [file]. I answer what it prints / where the bug is and why. Don't confirm until I commit to an answer. If I'm wrong, make me explain the actual mechanism before moving on.
> **Claim → why → tradeoff → my project.**

readMore.why: The three drill modes in full.

items.title: G3: why the query uses the new threshold
items.body:
`nums.Where(n => n > threshold)` does not filter anything when it is written. It builds a query object that holds the lambda. The lambda captures the *variable* `threshold`, not its value at that time. The filtering happens only when `string.Join` enumerates the query, and by then `threshold` is 2. So only 3 passes `n > 2`. If you had added `.ToList()` on the query line, the filter would run immediately with threshold 1 and the result would be "2,3".

Why the others are wrong:
- 3 is greater than 2, so the result is not empty.
- "2,3" is what you get with `.ToList()` at definition (threshold still 1), not here.
- "1,2,3" would need no filtering at all; 1 is never greater than the threshold.

excerpts.quote: int threshold = 1; var nums = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 }; var query = nums.Where(n => n > threshold); threshold = 2; Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", query));
**Why:** deferred execution — the lambda reads `threshold` **when enumerated**, not when defined, and by then it's 2. Add `.ToList()` at definition and you get `2,3`.

items.title: G24: why the projection runs twice
items.body:
`q` is a deferred query: `Select` runs its lambda (which writes a star) every time something walks through the sequence. `q.Count()` walks all three items: three stars. `q.ToList()` walks them again: three more. Total six stars. Nothing is stored between the two passes, because `q` is a recipe, not a list. The guide's warning: this is harmless here but costly when the source is a database query (two round-trips) or has side effects. Call `ToList()` once and reuse the list.

Why the others are wrong:
- `Count()` on a `Select` over a plain range still enumerates here, as the guide's answer shows, so the lambda runs.
- `Count()` is not deferred; it returns a number, so it must run the query right away.
- `Select` does not cache results; every enumeration runs the projection again.

excerpts.quote: var q = Enumerable.Range(1, 3).Select(x => { Console.Write("*"); return x; }); var count = q.Count(); var list = q.ToList();

**Answer:** `******` then `6` **Why:** six stars — the sequence is enumerated **twice**, so the projection runs twice. Harmless with `Select`; catastrophic when the source is a database query (two round-trips) or has side effects. This is why you materialize once with `ToList()` when you'll use a result more than once.

items.title: G8: why == in a generic method compares references
items.body:
Operators like `==` are picked at **compile time**. Inside the generic `Eq` method the compiler only knows that `T` is some class (`where T : class`), so it compiles `a == b` once as reference equality: "are these the same object?". At runtime T is `string`, but the method is not recompiled, so string's own `==` (which compares characters) is never used. "hello" and `new string(...)` are two different objects, so the result is False. The fix is the guide's `EqualityComparer` call (`.Default.Equals(a, b)`), which calls the type's own equality.

Why the others are wrong:
- The second string is created with `new string(...)`, so it is a different object from the interned literal; interning does not make it true.
- With the `class` constraint, `==` compiles; it means reference equality.
- Operator choice happens at compile time, not at runtime, so string's overload is not used.

excerpts.quote: static bool Eq<T>(T a, T b) where T : class => a == b; Console.WriteLine(Eq("hello", new string(new[] { 'h','e','l','l','o' })));

**Why:** the `==` inside a generic method is compiled **once**, against the constraint (`class`), so it's reference equality — even when T turns out to be `string` at runtime. Fix: `EqualityComparer<T>.Default.Equals(a, b)`, which dispatches properly. This one catches very good developers.

items.title: G12: integer division and remainder with negative numbers
items.body:
In C#, `/` between two ints is integer division and **truncates toward zero**: -2.5 becomes -2, not -3. The remainder `%` takes the sign of the **dividend** (the left number), so `-5 % 2` is -1. The two fit together: (-2 × 2) + (-1) = -5. The guide notes that Python floors instead and gives -3 and 1, a real bug source when porting code.

Why the others are wrong:
- C# does not floor: -3 would be floor division.
- Both operands are `int`, so the result is an `int`; a negative sign does not turn anything into `double`. (`5 / 2.0` gives 2.5 because 2.0 is a double.)
- -3 and 1 is Python's behaviour, which the guide warns about.

excerpts.quote: Console.WriteLine(5 / 2); Console.WriteLine(5 / 2.0); Console.WriteLine(-5 / 2); Console.WriteLine(-5 % 2); ``` **Answer:** `2`, `2.5`, `-2`, `-1`

**Why:** integer division truncates **toward zero** (not floor — so `-5/2` is `-2`, not `-3`), and C#'s `%` takes the sign of the **dividend**. Python floors and gives `-3` and `1` — a real cross-language bug when porting.
